content: Frequent administration of large doses of glucagon can lead to significant nausea and vomiting, which further impairs the ability to consume food. Therefore, smaller doses may be more effective for managing less severe hypoglycemia caused by inadequate intake. A recommended dose is 10 mcg per year of age (with a minimum of 20 mcg and a maximum of 150 mcg). If there is no response within 30 minutes, a repeat dose at twice the initial amount can be attempted. Rapid-acting insulin should be administered at doses of 10% to 20% of the total daily insulin requirement every 3 to 4 hours until ketones are cleared. Additional fluids should be provided to maintain hydration and facilitate the excretion of excess glucose and ketoacids. Blood glucose and ketone levels should be monitored frequently, at least every 3 to 4 hours. During certain illnesses, the usual daily insulin doses, adjusted for food intake and glucose concentrations, can be continued. For illnesses that disrupt oral intake and lead to ketone development, treatment with more frequent, smaller doses of insulin is recommended. Typical doses may range from 5% to 10% of the total daily dose every 3 to 4 hours, increasing to 10% to 20% of the total daily dose every 3 to 4 hours if ketones are present. In hypoglycemic episodes, care must be taken to avoid inducing hypoglycemia in a child who cannot consume sufficient calories due to illness. If solid foods cannot be eaten, sugar-containing foods such as soda, juice, gelatin desserts, and popsicles can be provided to maintain caloric intake and prevent hypoglycemia. For significant hypoglycemia during illness, the usual dose of glucagon must be administered. However, because these doses often cause nausea and vomiting, which further compromise food intake, smaller doses may be more effective for less severe hypoglycemia. A dose of 10 mcg per year of age (minimum 20 mcg, maximum 150 mcg) is recommended, with a repeat dose at twice the amount if there is no response within 30 minutes. In children not known to have diabetes but presenting with vomiting and dehydration, particularly in the presence of altered sensorium or in the absence of other viral infection indicators such as fever and diarrhea, diabetes should be considered. It should also be considered in cases with a preceding history of polydipsia and polyuria. For diabetic children, ketones should be measured when the child is significantly ill, vomiting, or experiencing persistent hyperglycemia. During a ketotic illness, referral for medical care should be considered if the patient begins vomiting. Medical attention is necessary if the patient exhibits deep respirations or is unable to stand. Early identification and treatment are critical to minimizing further risks and complications. Associated Autoimmune Diseases Thyroid Dysfunction: Thyroid dysfunction occurs more frequently in individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) should be measured shortly after the diagnosis of diabetes and subsequently every 1 to 2 years. TSH should also be measured whenever thyroid-related signs or symptoms develop. Thyroxine concentrations and thyroid antibodies may also be assessed. Celiac Disease: Celiac disease is more common in children with T1DM. All patients should be screened at least once and whenever poor growth or gastrointestinal symptoms are reported. Tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies are more sensitive and specific than antigliadin antibodies. It is also important to ensure that the patient is not IgA-deficient by measuring IgA concentrations, as these antibodies are immunoglobulin A (IgA)-based. Growth Disturbance Height and weight should be measured at every appointment and plotted on growth curves to detect deviations from normal growth velocities early. Decreased growth velocity, downward crossing of percentiles for height and weight, eventual short stature, and delayed skeletal and sexual maturation are associated with chronic undertreatment with insulin. Poor diabetic control negatively affects linear growth. Mauriac Syndrome or Diabetic Dwarfism: This rare and extreme form of growth disturbance is usually associated with hepatomegaly. Conversely, treatment with excessive insulin doses often leads to excessive weight gain, causing the weight curve to cross percentiles upward. Therefore, maintaining normal growth curves for height and weight is an important goal of diabetes management. Retinopathy Diabetic retinopathy is usually not observed before 5 to 10 years of diabetes duration. Risk factors include poor metabolic control, elevated blood pressure, smoking, albuminuria, and elevated lipid levels. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends the first ophthalmologic examination once the child is at least 10 years old and/or has had diabetes for 3 to 5 years. Annual follow-up examinations are suggested thereafter. Nephropathy All patients with T1DM should be monitored for nephropathy through annual urine microalbumin testing, beginning after the child is 10 years old and has had diabetes for 5 years. This is due to the increased risk of developing end-stage renal disease, which may require dialysis or transplantation. Hypertension accelerates the progression of nephropathy; therefore, blood pressure should be monitored several times a year, and hypertension should be treated aggressively. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are recommended for the treatment of hypertension. Microalbuminuria (30–299 mg of albumin per gram of creatinine on spot urine) is a marker for early nephropathy.
